title: Can architects claim R&D tax credits?
description: Architecture firms can claim the federal R&D credit under IRC section 41 for technical design work that resolves genuine uncertainty.
summary: Architecture firms in the United States can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC section 41, but only for technical design work that resolves genuine uncertainty through engineering analysis, modeling, simulation or testing. Aesthetic choices and routine code compliance do not qualify, and recent cases show contract terms and detailed time records often decide eligibility.

body.text: Architecture firms in the United States can claim the federal R&D tax credit under IRC section 41, but only for technical design work that resolves genuine uncertainty through engineering analysis, modeling, simulation or testing. Aesthetic choices and routine code compliance do not qualify, and recent cases show contract terms and detailed time records often decide eligibility.
This report is general information, not tax or legal advice.
Summary

Yes. Architecture firms can claim the federal credit for increasing research activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) section 41, but only for specific technical work that meets the statutory tests, not for architecture as a profession. Design work qualifies when the firm faced genuine uncertainty about how to make a building system function, evaluated alternatives through engineering analysis, modeling, simulation or testing, and can trace its costs to that evaluation. Aesthetic choices, routine code-compliance work and standard deliverables do not qualify on their own.

In the United States, the deciding issues in recent architecture and engineering cases have been two. The first is whether the client "funded" the research under the firm's contract. The second is whether the firm's records show a process of experimentation for substantially all of the claimed activity. The Tax Court upheld an architectural firm's position on fixed-price contracts in 2019 (Populous Holdings). Later decisions narrowed that result: Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (Eighth Circuit, 2024) and Smith v. Commissioner (Tax Court, June 2026) require contract terms that tie payment to the success of the research, and Smith adds that contracts transferring copyright and project data to the client can leave the firm without the substantial rights it needs. Phoenix Design Group (Tax Court, 2024) denied an engineering firm's credits because its time records could not show experimentation.
Who can claim
United Kingdom (comparison only)

GOV.UK guidance states that only companies chargeable to UK Corporation Tax can qualify, and that the project must seek an advance in a field of science or technology by resolving scientific or technological uncertainty. That guidance distinguishes accounting periods beginning before April 1, 2024 from those beginning on or after that date, when the merged R&D expenditure credit scheme took effect, and links to separate pages for each relief.
United States

Section 41(a) grants the credit to "the taxpayer," a term that covers C corporations, S corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies taxed under any of those regimes, and sole proprietors. The IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) state that partnerships and S corporations must file Form 6765 to claim the credit, while owners whose only source of the credit is a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust generally report their share on Form 3800, General Business Credit, without filing Form 6765 themselves. Many architecture practices are organized as partnerships or limited liability partnerships; the June 2026 Smith case discussed below concerned exactly such a firm, Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP, whose partners claimed the credit through the partnership.

Small and newer firms have an additional route. A qualified small business, defined in section 41(h)(3) as a taxpayer with gross receipts of less than $5 million for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year before the five-tax-year period ending with that year, may elect to apply up to $500,000 of the credit each year against the employer share of Social Security tax (and, for tax years beginning after 2022, Medicare tax) instead of income tax. This matters for young practices that have payroll but little or no income tax liability.
The US statutory test for qualified research

Section 41(d)(1)(A), as amended by Public Law 119-21, requires that the expenditures be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A; before that amendment, the reference was to specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174. In Phoenix Design Group, the IRS contested both this test and the process-of-experimentation test.
Section 174A expenditure test

Section 174A, added for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, allows taxpayers to deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures currently, or to elect to capitalize and amortize them over at least 60 months under section 174A(c). For the research credit, the relevant point is the definition, not the timing: the costs must be research or experimental expenditures in the experimental or laboratory sense, meaning costs incident to developing or improving a product where the information available does not establish the capability, method or appropriate design (Treas. Reg. section 1.174-2(a)(1)). For an architecture firm, the "product" is typically the design of a building system or component. Foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under section 174 and do not qualify for the credit in any event because section 41(d)(4)(F) excludes research conducted outside the United States. Revenue Procedure 2025-28 sets out the procedures and transition options for adopting section 174A, including the option for eligible small businesses (average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less) to apply the new rules retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021.
Permitted purpose

Section 41(d)(3)(A) treats research as having a qualified purpose when it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality of the business component. Section 41(d)(3)(B) provides that research is not treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors. The practical consequence is that a firm must separate the engineering problem (for example, whether a cantilevered floor plate can meet deflection limits, or whether a façade assembly can meet a thermal performance target) from the visual intent that created it. The visual intent may be the reason the problem exists, but only the work to resolve the functional problem can qualify.
Elimination of technical uncertainty

Treasury Regulation section 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) provides that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, and that uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. Section 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) adds that the taxpayer need not seek information that exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field; the discovery test that once required that kind of advance was removed by the 2004 final regulations.

The "competent professional" and "system uncertainty" standards are UK rules. Both come from the UK Guidelines on the Meaning of Research and Development for Tax Purposes (the Department for Business, Innovation and Skills Guidelines, reproduced in HMRC manual CIRD81900). Paragraph 13 of those Guidelines describes uncertainty as existing when the relevant knowledge is not readily available or deducible by a competent professional working in the field, and paragraph 29 defines system uncertainty as uncertainty resulting from the complexity of a system rather than its individual components. The US regulation measures uncertainty by the information available to the taxpayer instead, and the federal rules have no separate "system uncertainty" concept, although the shrinking-back rule in Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(b)(2) lets a taxpayer apply the tests to a larger business component first and then to successively smaller subsets. A UK claim should be framed around the competent-professional test; a US claim should be framed around Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(3).
Process of experimentation

Section 41(d)(1)(C) requires that substantially all of the activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The regulations define a process of experimentation as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain at the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities (Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)). The process fundamentally relies on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering or computer science, and may involve modeling, simulation or a systematic trial-and-error methodology. The "substantially all" requirement is met only if 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, are elements of a process of experimentation (Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(6)).
Technological in nature

Under section 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering or computer science. For architects, the relevant disciplines are usually structural engineering, building physics (heat, air and moisture transfer), acoustics, fluid dynamics for wind and ventilation, and materials science.

body.text: Telling routine design from qualified research

The Tax Adviser's September 2025 analysis of Phoenix Design Group makes the same point with a specific example: the firm could have recorded its initial HVAC sizing uncertainties and the airflow analyses that followed as distinct work, separate from routine code-compliance calculations. That article also lists consultations with manufacturers as an investigative step and recommends logging each modeling iteration with its quantitative result.

Section 41(d)(4) also lists exclusions that bear directly on design practice. Adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirements (section 41(d)(4)(B)) and duplicating an existing business component (section 41(d)(4)(C)) are not qualified research. A firm that reuses a proven structural or envelope solution on a new site, adjusting only dimensions and loads within known methods, is performing adaptation, not research. The regulations also exclude routine data collection and routine quality-control testing (Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(3), (c)).

Analysis. Each still needs evidence that the design was uncertain at the outset, that alternatives were evaluated, and that the firm's costs can be traced to that evaluation. Equally, a project the firm considers routine can contain a qualifying subcomponent, such as a novel connection detail or an unusual ventilation strategy, which the shrinking-back rule allows the firm to claim on its own.
Examples
These are marketing materials, not tax authority determinations, and they show what advisers have claimed, not what the IRS has accepted on examination.

items: Laboratory science building (Anchin). Anchin describes a firm with no prior experience of scientific-lab criteria that designed a university laboratory building to LEED standards. Vibration control for sensitive equipment was a major area of experimentation, and wind turbines were installed and later removed during that work.

Spine-like lateral system (Anchin). The same project included a spine-like lateral support system using cables for a two-story glass curtain wall, an approach Anchin says the company had never attempted before.
MEP design adapted for public access and safety (Source Advisors). The case study concerns a construction firm with MEP engineering capabilities.

Alternative structural designs and materials (Frazier & Deeter, formerly the GGG article cited). The article lists determining alternative structural designs, alternative materials (with pre-stressed concrete and glass as examples), alternative means of assembling or fastening parts, and designing building shape and form.

body.text: Funded research: the contract question
The rule

Section 41(d)(4)(H) excludes "any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)." The regulations treat all agreements between the researcher and others as relevant, and provide that amounts payable under an agreement that are contingent on the success of the research, and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research, are not treated as funding (Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4A(d)(1)). Separately, research in which the taxpayer retains no substantial rights is treated as fully funded (section 1.41-4A(d)(2)), and where the taxpayer retains substantial rights the research is funded to the extent of the payments, and the taxpayer must reduce its qualified research expenses accordingly (section 1.41-4A(d)(3)). Incidental benefits, such as the knowledge and experience the firm gains, do not count as substantial rights on their own.
Populous Holdings (2019): fixed-price architectural contracts

That case is Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Tax Court Docket No. 405-17, an order granting the taxpayer partial summary judgment dated December 6, 2019. The court reviewed five representative fixed-price contracts, found that the firm bore the economic risk of failed research because it would not be paid if its designs did not meet the contract requirements, and found that it retained substantial rights because it could use the research results in other work. It held the research was not funded. The Eighth Circuit's later opinion in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson quotes the order's statement that fixed-price contracts have generally been considered unfunded research. As an unpublished order, Populous Holdings is not precedential.
Meyer, Borgman & Johnson (2024): fixed price is not enough

In Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, No. 23-1523, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024), the Eighth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's summary judgment denying a structural engineering firm about $190,000 in credits for its tax years ending September 30, 2010, 2011 and 2013. The court found that none of the contracts tied payment, expressly or by clear implication, to the success of the research. It distinguished meeting codes or a general professional standard of care ("proper performance") from successful performance of the research, noted the absence of refund provisions or rejection rights tied to specific benchmarks, and, following the Fifth Circuit in Dynetics and Grigsby, held that a fixed-price structure alone does not make research unfunded. The opinion is binding in the Eighth Circuit and has been followed by the Tax Court elsewhere.
Update: Smith v. Commissioner (June 2026), an architectural firm

In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (June 16, 2026; Docket Nos. 13382-17 and consolidated cases), the partners of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP, an Illinois architectural firm known for supertall towers, challenged the disallowance of research credits for the firm's 2008 through 2010 tax years. According to the taxpayer's counsel, the IRS conceded that the work met the four-part test, so the dispute centered on the funded-research exclusion. The court applied a two-step analysis across six sample projects.

items: Substantial rights. For two projects, the contracts transferred copyright to the client, made project data the client's absolute property, and required the client's express prior written approval before the firm could use project information for another purpose. The firm therefore retained no substantial rights, and the research on those projects was treated as fully funded.

Financial risk. For the other four projects, the firm kept substantial rights, but payments tied to monthly progress or completion of design phases were not contingent on research success. Relying on Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, the court held that payment is contingent on success only where the contract sets specific, measurable success criteria. The research was therefore partially funded.

Effect of partial funding. The court did not award a partial credit amount. Under Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4A(d)(3), the firm can claim credit only to the extent its qualified research expenses on each of those projects exceeded the client's payments, and it bears the burden of proving that excess.

Loper Bright challenge. The court rejected the argument that the funded-research regulations lost their force after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), and upheld Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4A(d).
Reasonable compensation. The court also held that the partners' compensation counted as reasonable for purposes of section 174(e), applying the Seventh Circuit's independent-investor test.

body.text: Standard owner-architect agreements that assign copyright or instruments of service to the owner, or bill by design phase, should be reviewed before a claim is filed.

body.text: Documentation: what the cases require
Phoenix Design Group (2024)

Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, filed December 23, 2024), involved a multidisciplinary engineering consulting firm (MEP design) that claimed credits for research years 2013 through 2016 across more than 200 projects. The parties tried a nonbinding sample of three projects, and the court held that none was qualified research. It rejected the firm's six-stage design process as proof of experimentation, holding that connecting an activity to a larger plan that resembles the scientific method is not enough. The firm's hour sheets were an internal performance metric, were not categorized by design phase, and could not be tied to specific design issues, so the court could not verify that the work was experimental or apply the shrinking-back rule. The firm was liable for accuracy-related penalties under section 6662 under the parties' stipulation.
Harper

The case is Harper v. United States, 847 F. App'x 408 (9th Cir. 2021). Jeffrey Harper, sole shareholder of Harper Construction Co., filed refund claims supported by more than 100,000 pages of documentation. The district court dismissed the suit on the ground that the refund claims lacked the specificity Treas. Reg. section 301.6402-2(b)(1) requires. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the IRS had waived that procedural objection by accepting the properly filed Form 6765 and examining the merits of the claim over several years. The taxpayer prevailed on a procedural waiver. The case does not hold that the documentation was insufficient, and it should not be cited as a documentation-quality precedent. Its practical lesson is narrower: the IRS can raise specificity objections to refund claims, which is one reason it later issued formal refund-claim requirements.
Current documentation rules

Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(d) requires a taxpayer claiming the credit to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit.

items: For research credit refund claims filed on or after January 10, 2022, Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F requires the claim to identify all business components to which the credit relates, describe the research activities performed and the individuals who performed them for each business component, describe the information each individual sought to discover, and state the total qualified wage, supply and contract research expenses. In June 2024 the IRS relaxed the second and third items so that the names of individuals and the information each sought to discover need not be provided at filing, although they may be requested on examination.

The Form 6765 instructions (Rev. December 2025, finalized in February 2026) make Section G, the business component information section, optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025. Two exceptions apply: a qualified small business under section 41(h)(3) that elects the reduced payroll tax credit, and a taxpayer whose total QREs determined at the controlled group level are $1.5 million or less, whose average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years are $50 million or less, and who reports the credit on an original return.

body.text: Analysis. For an architecture firm, Phoenix Design Group shows that time records coded only to a project, or to labels such as "design," will not carry the 80 percent substantially-all test. Time coded to the specific technical question and to each modeling or testing iteration is what the court found missing. Section G now asks for comparable information at the filing stage for most claimants with more than $1.5 million in QREs, so firms above that threshold should expect to report business-component data on the return itself starting with 2026 tax years.
What expenses count, and what the credit is worth

Section 41(b) defines qualified research expenses as in-house research expenses (wages paid for qualified services, supplies used in the research, and amounts paid to another person for the right to use computers in the research) plus contract research expenses, which are generally included at 65 percent of amounts paid to non-employees for qualified research (section 41(b)(3)(A)), or 75 percent for payments to a qualified research consortium. Consultant payments therefore count at 65 percent, not in full, and only if the firm bears the financial risk of the consultant's research and retains substantial rights in it (Treas. Reg. section 1.41-2(e)). Modeling software purchases or licenses are not a listed category; only computer-use payments to another person are. Wages qualify for employees who perform, directly supervise or directly support qualified research (section 41(b)(2)(B)); for partners, guaranteed payments and distributive shares are not wages for this purpose, which limits the credit for firms where partners perform much of the technical work.

The credit rate is 20 percent of qualified research expenses above a base amount under the regular method (section 41(a)(1)). Under the alternative simplified credit (section 41(c)(4)), the credit is 14 percent of qualified research expenses exceeding 50 percent of the average for the three preceding tax years, or 6 percent of current-year qualified research expenses where the taxpayer had no qualified research expenses in any one of those three years. Under section 280C(c) as amended by Public Law 119-21, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, a taxpayer must reduce its section 174A domestic research deduction by the amount of the credit unless it elects a reduced credit on a timely filed original return; the reduced credit equals the full credit multiplied by 79 percent (100 percent minus the 21 percent corporate rate). The credit reduces tax dollar for dollar, but its use in a given year is subject to the general business credit limitation in section 38(c), with unused amounts carried back one year and forward 20 years under section 39.

Specialist advisers

Any paid preparer of a research credit claim is subject to the preparer penalty rules in section 6694 and the practice standards in Treasury Department Circular 230, and the taxpayer remains liable for accuracy-related penalties under section 6662 if a claim is disallowed, as the stipulated penalties in Phoenix Design Group show.
Analysis. Whether any particular adviser is the best choice is a commercial judgment that this report does not verify.
Practical steps for architecture firms
These steps follow from the law and cases above and are analysis, not statements of law.

items: Identify projects where the design was uncertain at the outset under Treas. Reg. section 1.41-4(a)(3), and exclude work driven by style or appearance under section 41(d)(3)(B), as well as adaptation or duplication of existing designs under section 41(d)(4)(B) and (C).
Record time by technical question and by iteration, so the 80 percent substantially-all test can be measured, and keep the modeling, simulation and test results that show the alternatives evaluated.

Review contract terms for both funded-research tests: whether payment depends on specific, measurable success criteria, and whether the firm keeps the right to use its research results without paying for them. After Smith, phase-based fees, copyright assignment and client ownership of design data are risk factors, and clauses that let the firm reuse its technical know-how help.
Review consultant agreements the same way, because contract research counts at 65 percent only where the firm bears the risk and retains substantial rights.
Decide each year whether to make the section 280C(c) reduced-credit election on the original return, and, for qualified small businesses, whether to make the payroll tax election.

For tax years beginning after 2025, plan to complete Form 6765 Section G unless an exception applies, and for refund claims on amended returns, follow the business-component requirements that apply to claims filed on or after January 10, 2022.
For UK claims, frame uncertainty around the competent-professional test in the Guidelines, and confirm the scheme that applies to the accounting period.
